# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Before copying anything, read `techniques.md` and every file in
`.claude/rules/` (`hacks.md`, `x11shim.md`, `device-display.md`, `gl.md`,
`tools-scoring.md`) in full. The gotchas live there, and a harness may not load
them for you (`.pi/rules` links to the same directory for pi).

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Xft text (`XftDrawStringUtf8`) | Xft text (XJack) |
| Threads, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. For a
single-precision wrapper, also build for the device and run
`uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>`: a count in a per-frame function is
a literal, macro or struct the rename missed (`techniques.md`). Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such. After a
batch, log one 20 s-a-hack rotation lap and run `tools/triage_hacks.py`
(`hacks.md` says how): it shows which hacks are step-bound, push-bound or paced
by their own delay, with their soft-double calls, so a slow hack is looked at
for the right reason.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Done means

A port is done on the host only when all of these hold: a dumped frame viewed
at two or more frame counts (with seeds forced if the hack picks a mode); a
leak test, mutation-checked; the largest stack frame measured; the hash pinned
from a frame you looked at; and a notices row that matches each file's header.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |
| "Dump with 0 and 5 frames exits cleanly, so it works" | That shows it starts and stops, not what it draws. Convert a frame to PNG and look. |
| "A `0` in `kBaseline` keeps the suite green" | It also stops the suite checking a single frame. Use `0x1ull` until you have looked, then pin. |
| "A hook will not run, so `--no-verify`" | That skips ruff, markdownlint and gitleaks. `SKIP=<hook>`, and say so in the PR. |

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: `.venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file>
  <seconds> [port]` reads `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 into a file and
  reopens the port when it goes away. Run it in the background with absolute
  paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  `serial_capture.py` sets `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened
  `serial.Serial()` before `open()`, as any script of your own must: a reopen
  loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- The port name changes with the USB socket the board is plugged into
  (`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` became `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14). When
  it is missing, find the board without touching it:
  `ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product
  Name|USB Serial Number"` lists USB devices, and
  `ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice` lists the serial
  ports. The StopWatch is the "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" from Espressif
  (`idVendor` 12346, `idProduct` 4097). Its USB serial number is its MAC:
  Rod's board is `28:84:85:43:B2:70`, so check that before flashing a port
  you have not used before. Pass `--upload-port <port>` to `pio run -t upload`
  and read the same port for the serial log, and leave `platformio.ini`'s
  `upload_port` alone. Still ask Rod before each flash. The auto-mode
  classifier refused a flash to an overridden port once: give Rod the command
  to run with `!`.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

20	---
21	
22	# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas
23	
24	OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
25	`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.
26	
27	- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
28	  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
29	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
30	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
31	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
32	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
33	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
34	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
35	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
36	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
37	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
38	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
39	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
40	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
41	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
42	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
43	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
44	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
45	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
46	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
47	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
48	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
49	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
50	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
51	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
52	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
53	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
54	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
55	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
56	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
57	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
58	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
59	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
60	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
61	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
62	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
63	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
64	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
65	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
66	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
67	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
68	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing: Rubik's wrapper (`rubik_gl.c`) draws its
69	  convex octagon stickers as a triangle fan, and with a polygon offset, since
70	  a sticker is 0.01 above its cube face, about two 16-bit depth steps at the
71	  cube's distance, and the face showed through in patches (7,152 coloured
72	  pixels in the pinned frame, 8,678 with the offset). Unknown Pleasures' rim
73	  loop is drawn too, but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face
74	  (-0.01), so no frame changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting
75	  vertices, and the fifth overwrote the matrices and colours after
76	  `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c` crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now
77	  holds it at the first slot. Check a new hack for both.
78	- A decal drawn a hair above a surface z-fights with it at 16-bit depth, and a
79	  test that only asks whether something drew passes. Count the decal's
80	  coloured pixels, and mutation-check the offset (`test_hacks.c`'s Rubik
81	  sticker test fails at 7,152 without it).
82	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
83	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
84	  neither.
85	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
86	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
87	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
88	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
89	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
90	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
91	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
92	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
93	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
94	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
95	- Unknown Pleasures runs at `*speed: 0.3` (a registry override; the panel dims
96	  after each push by an amount that grows with the scroll per push, see
97	  `device-display.md` and issue #68). The hack halves `*count` at displays of
98	  480 pixels or less, so the default of 80 draws 40 rows and `*count: 40` draws
99	  20. Every new row is added by `tick_unk` (about every 1.2 s at full speed).
100	  Upstream adds it at the end of a draw and restarts its clock at that frame's
101	  time, and the frame was drawn at the scroll's clamp, so the time past the
102	  interval never scrolled: the picture stood still for a push (issue #134,
103	  filmed as a 190 ms stall every seventh push at 40 rows of 50 points).
104	  `unknownpleasures_gl.c` adds the row before the draw and moves the clock on
105	  by one interval. The tick is 12 to 35 ms (software `double` `cos`) and the
106	  TE sync wait absorbs it, so it never stretched a frame. `glLineWidth` is a
107	  no-op in the shim.
108	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
109	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
110	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
111	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
112	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
113	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
114	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
115	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
116	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
117	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
118	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
119	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
120	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
121	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
122	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
123	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
124	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
125	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
126	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
127	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
128	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
129	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
130	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
131	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.17 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only
  appears when there are any). Failures are recorded in
  `tools/failed_ports.txt`.

## Effort ratings

| Rating | Meaning | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | 2D, and the unmodified source compiles against the shim | 3 |
| M | 2D, 1-4 shim gaps, no pixmaps or pixel read-back | 1 |
| L | 2D, 5+ shim gaps, or uses pixmaps or pixel read-back | 40 |
| XL | GL: runs on the TinyGL layer, each hack needs its own GL calls and helpers checked (see below) | 129 |
| Ported | Already running on the device, so no rating | 110 |

## Speed

result.output:
# GL budget: cubicgrid and morph3d

`tools/gl_budget.py` runs a GL hack on the host, counts what each frame asks of
TinyGL, and predicts the device frame time. It was built to choose between two
candidates for the next GL port (issue #45) without flashing either.

```text
uv run tools/gl_budget.py [--frames N] [--seeds a,b,c]
    [--override '*name: value' ...] name[:seed] ...
```

Gears is read from `firmware/src/hacks/gears/`; any other name from
`vendor/xscreensaver-6.17/hacks/glx/` (git-ignored, never copied into the
repo). A hack that does not build is reported with its first error, and the
exit status is 1.

`--override` gives the hack a resource line that beats its own defaults, as an
entry in `registry.c`'s override list does on the device. Repeat it for more.
It applies to every hack named, so run hacks with different overrides
separately. Use it to try a registry override (`--override '*count: 40'`)
before committing to it, or to supply one a hack needs to start.

## What it counts

The counters sit inside a private copy of TinyGL, built only for the tool
(`firmware/src/tinygl/` and the firmware builds are untouched). Counting there
means a display list that is built once and replayed every frame is counted on
every frame. Per frame, it records:

- **Vertices** set up, and how many of them were lit.
- **Triangles** rasterised, after back-face culling, and the **pixels** they
  cover (screen area, overdraw included, capped at the canvas).
- **Lines** and **points** drawn.

## The cost model

A frame costs a fixed 56.6 ms (clear 24.6 ms, display push 32 ms), plus 4 us
per vertex, 2.8 us more for each enabled light on each lit vertex (both from the
Pipes probe in #43, measured with one light), plus a fill term. The fill term
is 570 ns a pixel, fitted so that the heavy Gears scene (seed 13, 17,700
vertices) costs the 40 ms of fill that #43 measured.

Checked against Gears, the only hack with device numbers. The fit and the
tests use 60 frames; the table below is a 300 frame run, and Gears' pixel
count drifts by about 15 percent between the two as the gears turn (at 60
frames the heavy scene is 217 ms and its fill is exactly 40 ms; at 300 it is
211 ms and 34 ms):

| Scene | Predicted | Measured (#43) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gears seed 13, heavy | 211 ms, 4.7 fps | 197 to 217 ms, about 5 fps |
| Gears seed 11, light (held out) | 117 ms, 8.5 fps | about 111 ms, 9 fps |

The light scene was not used in the fit and lands within 6 percent.

## The comparison

Means over 300 frames after a 10 frame warm-up. Both hacks are lit or point
based, so the fixed 56.6 ms sets a ceiling of about 17.7 fps for anything.

                        a resource line that beats the hack's defaults, as a
                        registry override does on the device; repeat for more,
                        applies to every hack named
  --seeds SEEDS         comma-separated seeds tried for each hack without its
                        own

"""PlatformIO pre-build script: converts the textures GL hacks load
(BlockTube's blocktube.png) into the raw blobs they include as
images/gen/<name>_png.h (see src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h for the
format), as matrix_glyphs.py does for XMatrix, and puts them on the include
path. The images are read from vendor/ and never committed. Needs uv, because
Pillow is not in PlatformIO's Python."""

import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

repo = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"]).parent  # noqa: F821
sys.path.insert(0, str(repo / "tools"))
import xs_vendor

images = xs_vendor.upstream(repo) / "hacks" / "images"
converter = repo / "tools" / "make_logo_blob.py"
generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821

for name in ("blocktube",):
    image = images / f"{name}.png"
    header = generated / "images" / "gen" / f"{name}_png.h"
    if not image.is_file():
        sys.exit(f"{image} is missing: run `uv run tools/fetch_xscreensaver.py`")
    if (
        header.exists()
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= image.stat().st_mtime
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= converter.stat().st_mtime
    ):
        continue
    uv = shutil.which("uv")
    if not uv:
        raise SystemExit("gl_textures.py needs uv on PATH to convert the textures")
    header.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Written beside the header and renamed, so a killed build never leaves a
    # truncated header that the mtime check above would trust.
    partial = header.with_name(header.name + ".partial")
    partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    subprocess.run(
        [
            uv,
            "run",
            str(converter),
            str(image),
            "--name",
            f"{name}_png",
            "-o",
            str(partial),
        ],
        check=True,
    )
    os.replace(partial, header)

env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821

- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
  for each large hack.

## Images

Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
bitmap. There is no PNG
decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.

A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.

## Pixmap double buffering

When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)

- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.

## Restart leak test

When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.

Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.

On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.

## Stopping before the first draw

When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
frames exited 139.

- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).

## Tests that cannot be fooled

A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.

A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
old start.

# Working in a git worktree

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. It refuses `git ... | tar` and `cd <dir> && git ...`
  too: use `git archive -o f.tar <sha>` then `tar -x -f f.tar -C <dir>`, and run
  git from the worktree root. A background shell starts there as well, so use
  `pio test -d <abs>/firmware` with absolute paths. Parallel calls can race
  (a `uv run` in the root disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran:
  "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`. If no checkout has `main` out,
  `git fetch origin main:main` fast-forwards it from anywhere.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone. After a merge,
  `ExitWorktree keep` names a branch (`worktree-<name>`) that may not exist:
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` and delete the
  real branch, as separate commands, because a failed `&&` link skips the rest
  silently. Check `git worktree list` afterwards. `git worktree remove --force`
  fails on a worktree this session's harness locked ("cannot remove a locked
  working tree, lock reason: claude session"): once the tip is an ancestor of
  `origin/main`, `ExitWorktree remove` with `discard_changes: true` works, and
  its "discarded N commits" are the merged ones. In a session resumed from a
  summary, `ExitWorktree` can be a no-op ("no active EnterWorktree session"):
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` from the main
  checkout instead. To delete the merged branch
  you are standing on, `git switch --detach origin/main` in the worktree first.
  The shell's directory resets after each command and after `ExitWorktree`, so
  use absolute paths (`../.venv/bin/pio` failed from the wrong place and the run
  looked like a test failure). A loop over several mutations is refused as a
  command: write it as a script in the scratchpad that edits the file, runs
  `pio test` through `subprocess` and restores the file in `finally`, then run
  it with `python3 -I`.
  Stopping such a script (TaskStop) kills it before `finally` runs: check
  `git diff` afterwards and restore the file by hand.
  Also refused: a heredoc (use the Write tool for a scratchpad script), `$(...)`
  inside a git command, and the quoted `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` above combined
  with a redirect or `NO_COLOR=1`. Flashing worked as
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<wt>/.platformio PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="..."
  .venv/bin/pio run -d firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` with no redirect: the
  540 KB of output lands in a tool-results file, so grep that for "Hash of data
  verified". Edit and Write refuse the main checkout's path while you are in a
  worktree. `pio test -f test_x` runs the whole suite (`test_hacks` takes 3
  minutes, the full native run 7), and a failing summary reads "2 failed, 101
  succeeded": match `[FAILED]` or the return code, not "succeeded".
- `uv run ty check` (the pre-commit `ty` hook) fails in a worktree with
  "Failed to spawn: ty": the shared `.venv` has no `ty`. Run
  `uvx ty check --python .venv` instead (it passes on a clean tree), then
  commit with `SKIP=ty git commit ...`, and say in the PR that the hook was
  skipped. `ruff-format` rewrites a file and aborts the commit when a line is
  too long: restage the file and commit again.
- Also refused in a worktree session: a shell variable used as a program's
  argument (`S=...; prog $S/x`), a `for` loop that runs `uv` or `pio`, and
  `entire trail finding resolve -m "..."` text containing `*` or backticks.
  Spell out absolute paths, run one command per call, and keep `-m` text to
  plain words.

    i = text.find(marker)

    return text[:i] + addition + text[i:]


# The After Dark toasters stay last (built only with the disk image), so a new

GUARD = "#ifdef HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS\n"


def _guard_in(text: str, start: str, end: str) -> int:

  extern struct xscreensaver_function_table NAME##_xscreensaver_function_table; \
  static const HackEntry NAME##_hack = {                                 \
      CLASS, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL,                                     \
      &NAME##_xscreensaver_function_table, OVERRIDES, SYNC, LINE32, REPAINTS}
#define XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH(NAME, CLASS, OVERRIDES) \
  XLOCKMORE_HACK_FULL(NAME, CLASS, OVERRIDES, 0, 0, 0)

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("/Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver")
name, cls, copyright_text = sys.argv[1:4]
cmd = [
    "uv", "run", "tools/wire_hack.py", name, cls, copyright_text,
    "--glx", "--xlockmore",
]
if len(sys.argv) > 4:
    cmd += ["--notice", sys.argv[4]]
subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=root, check=True)

ini = root / "firmware" / "platformio.ini"
text = ini.read_text()
anchor = "-<hacks/rubik/>"
assert text.count(anchor) == 3, text.count(anchor)
text = text.replace(anchor, f"{anchor} -<hacks/{name}/> -<hacks/{name}_gl.c>")
ini.write_text(text)

wrapper = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / f"{name}_gl.c"
wrapper.write_text(
    f"/* Builds the unmodified {name}.c with USE_GL set for this file only, so no\n"
    " * other hack sees a GL build. See hacks/gears_gl.c. */\n"
    "#define USE_GL\n"
    f'#include "{name}/{name}.c"\n'
)
print("ok", name)

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.13"
# dependencies = ["pillow"]
# ///
"""Turn an image into the C header that Maze's logo is read from.

The device has no PNG decoder, so the image goes in as a raw RGB565 blob with
a 1-bit mask. The layout is documented in
firmware/src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h.

Run with: uv run tools/make_logo_blob.py logo-50.gif --name logo_50_png \\
    -o firmware/src/x11shim/include/images/gen/logo-50_png.h
"""

import argparse
import sys
import zlib
from pathlib import Path

OPAQUE_ALPHA = 128


def rgb565(r: int, g: int, b: int) -> int:
    return (r & 0xF8) << 8 | (g & 0xFC) << 3 | b >> 3


def build_blob(width: int, height: int, rgba: bytes) -> bytes:
    if not (0 < width <= 0xFFFF and 0 < height <= 0xFFFF):
        raise ValueError(f"size {width}x{height} does not fit the blob header")
    if len(rgba) != width * height * 4:
        raise ValueError(f"expected {width * height * 4} RGBA bytes, got {len(rgba)}")

    pixels = bytearray()
    mask = bytearray()
    stride = (width + 7) // 8
    for y in range(height):
        row = bytearray(stride)
        for x in range(width):
            r, g, b, a = rgba[(y * width + x) * 4 :][:4]
            opaque = a >= OPAQUE_ALPHA
            pixels += (rgb565(r, g, b) if opaque else 0).to_bytes(2, "little")
            if opaque:
                row[x // 8] |= 0x80 >> (x % 8)
        mask += row
    header = b"565M" + width.to_bytes(2, "little") + height.to_bytes(2, "little")
    return bytes(header + pixels + mask)


def deflate_blob(blob: bytes) -> bytes:
    """The "565Z" form: the same eight-byte header, then the pixels and mask as
    one zlib stream. The shim inflates it when a hack loads the image."""
    return b"565Z" + blob[4:8] + zlib.compress(blob[8:], 9)


def c_header(name: str, blob: bytes, source: str) -> str:
    guard = f"XSHIM_{name.upper()}_H"
    lines = []
    for i in range(0, len(blob), 12):
        lines.append("    " + ", ".join(f"0x{b:02x}" for b in blob[i : i + 12]) + ",")
    body = "\n".join(lines)

#!/bin/bash
# Flashes a build that starts on one hack with rotation off, then reads the
# serial log. Needs the board, and Rod's say-so in the session (AGENTS.md:
# never flash without asking, unless he has said it is allowed).
#
#   bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> <seconds> [extra build flags] [lines]
#
# <hack> is a name from g_hacks[] in any case; extra flags are things like
# "-DFIREWORKX_SCALE=2"; the last `run` lines (default 6) are printed. The full
# log and the flash output go to $OUT_DIR (default: ./flash-capture, which
# should be somewhere git ignores, such as your scratchpad).
set -u
[ $# -ge 2 ] || { sed -n '2,12p' "$0"; exit 2; }
hack=$1 seconds=$2 extra=${3:-} lines=${4:-6}
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
out=${OUT_DIR:-./flash-capture}
mkdir -p "$out"
out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)

source "$repo/tools/env.sh"
cd "$repo/firmware" || exit 1
PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="-DSTART_HACK=\\\"$hack\\\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=0 $extra" \
  NO_COLOR=1 pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > "$out/flash_$hack.txt" 2>&1
pio_status=$?
unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS
verified=$(grep -c 'Hash of data verified' "$out/flash_$hack.txt")

"""Makes the size of Etruscan Venus's surface grid a build setting.

Upstream draws the Klein bottle on a 192 by 128 grid and works out every point
and normal again each frame: about 25,000 points with ten sines and cosines
each, and 49,000 lit vertices. The board cannot do that at a useful rate, so
firmware/src/hacks/etruscanvenus_single_gl.c defines ETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU and
ETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV, and the build (firmware/patch_float_literals.py) runs this
on the hack's text. The copied etruscanvenus.c stays byte-identical. Each
replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build.
"""

REPLACEMENTS = [
    ("#define NUMU 192\n", "#define NUMU ETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU\n"),
    ("#define NUMV 128\n", "#define NUMV ETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV\n"),
]


def size_the_grid(source: str) -> str:
    for old, new in REPLACEMENTS:
        found = source.count(old)
        if found != 1:
            raise ValueError(
                f"expected 1 of `{old.strip()}` in etruscanvenus.c, found {found}; "
                "has upstream changed?"
            )
        source = source.replace(old, new)
    return source

/* Builds the unmodified deepstars.c with USE_GL set for this file only, so no
 * other hack sees a GL build. See hacks/gears_gl.c.
 *
 * Each smear copy of the sky is drawn at a lower alpha, blended over the one
 * before. TinyGL has no alpha, and its blend is right only for black and
 * white, so the wrapper folds the alpha into the colour and draws opaque:
 * `glColor4fv` scales its own colour, and the blend is never switched on. The
 * stars are at distinct places, so a dimmer copy only overwrites its own
 * brighter one where they touch.
 *
 * It also stops `glEnable(GL_POINT_SMOOTH)`, which TinyGL does not know and
 * prints a warning for every frame. */
#define USE_GL
#include "xlockmore.h"

static void deepstars_enable(GLenum cap) {
  if (cap != GL_BLEND && cap != GL_POINT_SMOOTH) glEnable(cap);
}

static void deepstars_color4fv(const GLfloat *c) {
  glColor3f(c[0] * c[3], c[1] * c[3], c[2] * c[3]);
}

#define glEnable deepstars_enable
#define glColor4fv deepstars_color4fv
#include "deepstars/deepstars.c"
EOF

"""Mutation-checks a file: breaks it one way at a time, runs the tests, and
reports whether they noticed.

    uv run tools/mutate.py <file> '<old>=><new>' ['<old>=><new>' ...] \\
        [--cmd 'pio test -e native -f test_float_polygon'] [--cwd firmware]

Each mutation replaces the first `<old>` in the file with `<new>`. A mutation is

- CAUGHT if the command fails with a test failure, a sanitizer report or a
  crash,
- BUILD ERROR if it fails without one (the mutation broke the compile: it proves
  nothing, so write a smaller one),
- SURVIVED if the command passes: the tests cannot tell the code from the
  broken code. Either a test is missing, or the mutation is equivalent (it
  changes nothing observable: say so rather than adding a test).

The file is always restored, and the run says so. Use `source tools/env.sh`
first for the default `pio` command. A multi-line mutation can be written with
real newlines inside the quotes.
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import shlex
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

BUILD_FAILURE = re.compile(
    r"\berror:|Building stage has failed|^\*\*\* \[.*\] Error \d+"
)

    "[FAILED]",
    "Sanitizer",
    "FAILED",
    "AssertionError",
    "Program received signal",  # a test crashed (ASan aborts print this under pio)
)

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

p='.claude/rules/hacks.md'
t=open(p).read()
t+='''- The 2026-10-18 GL batch (GLMatrix, CubeStack, Kaleidocycle, DangerBall,
  Cubenetic, DeepStars, Superquadrics, Menger) is eight `USE_GL` wrappers over
  unmodified sources. Most GL hacks wait 20-40 ms after a frame (`*delay`), and
  the loop credits only the push against it, so `kShortDelayOverrides` (10 ms)
  took CubeStack from 16.5 to 22 fps, Kaleidocycle 19.6 to 33 and DangerBall
  16.5 to 25 with no other change. Their motion is per frame, so it is faster
  too, nearer upstream's pace on a desktop.
- GLMatrix (`glmatrix_single_gl.c`) keeps its look in alpha: the texture's
  alpha is the glyph image's green channel and each glyph's brightness is the
  vertex alpha, drawn `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`. TinyGL has none, and the shim's
  `glTexImage2D` drops alpha, so glyph cells were solid green squares. The
  wrapper premultiplies the texture as it uploads and has `glColor4f` scale its
  colour: an additive blend cannot tell the difference. `xlockmore.h` must come
  before the `#define glTexImage2D` (it brings in `glshim.h`, whose macro would
  win). `matrix3.png` is deflated by `gl_textures.py` (`--deflate`). The step
  grows as the rain fills the screen (9 to 140 ms over about 80 s at full size)
  and fill is 100 of 145 ms: it renders at half size (`-DGLMATRIX_FULL` keeps
  full size) with `*density: 12` (26 strips, not 44) and `*delay: 10000`, about
  17 fps once full. Single precision gave byte-identical frames and about 3 ms.

content.text:
I ported eight GL hacks, GL Matrix included. The two commits are on `feature/gl-batch-7-glmatrix`, local only: nothing is pushed and there's no PR, since you didn't ask for one.

**What each one does on the board** (one 45 s rotation lap, eight windows each):

| Hack | fps range | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GLMatrix | 13-44 | about 17 once the screen is full; 6 as copied |
| CubeStack | 17-38 | |
| Kaleidocycle | 30-35 | |
| DangerBall | 24-26 | |
| Cubenetic | 12-18 | 1.2 fps as copied |
| DeepStars | 18-20 | 3-10 fps as copied |
| Superquadrics | 14-27 | 8-11 fps as copied |
| Menger | 13-44 | |

**GL Matrix:** it was the hard one. TinyGL has no alpha, and GL Matrix keeps its glyph shape and brightness in alpha, so at first every glyph was a solid green square. The wrapper now folds the alpha into the colour; an additive blend can't tell the difference. The remaining cost was fill, so it renders at half size with `*density: 12` and a 10 ms delay. It's chunkier than full size, and `-DGLMATRIX_FULL` restores full size at about 7 fps.

**Other fixes:**
- **Cubenetic** recomputed a 256×256 plasma texture every frame (847 ms). It's now 64×64 via a build-time patch.
- **Superquadrics and Menger** were black because TinyGL draws nothing for `GL_POLYGON` (issue #80). Each wrapper draws the quads as triangle fans, as Rubik does, and both render at half size. Menger's `*maxDepth` is capped at 2, because depth 3 took 920 ms a frame.
- **DeepStars** folds alpha into colour too. Its `*smear` is capped at 4, since upstream grows it to 400 copies of 2,700 stars (3.4 fps at 20). Its stars are dim by design.
- The three delay-paced hacks (CubeStack, Kaleidocycle, DangerBall) gained 30-70% from a 10 ms delay override alone.
- **A real upstream leak:** Cubenetic never frees its cube array (320 bytes a start). The restart leak test found it, and the wrapper now frees it.

**Verification:**
- **Host suite:** all 860 pass.
- **Mutation checks:** the mutations I tried on the new wrappers were caught.
- **Soak:** a 14-minute rotation at 5 s a hack showed no resets or panics. PSRAM and heap were identical on the second visit of each new hack.
- **FMA run:** with `-ffp-contract=off` the `test_hacks` run stops at XSpirograph, an older hack I didn't touch. The new pins weren't reached under that setting, and I didn't check whether main fails the same way.

**For you to look at:** the board is flashed with a rotating build (90 s per hack) that starts on GL Matrix. Only you can judge it by eye, mainly GL Matrix at half size and whether DeepStars is too dim.

**Not done:**
- **Cage and Moebius:** they need `e_textures.h` and a wood texture.
- **Shared `GL_POLYGON` fix:** two wrappers now work around issue #80 locally. A proper fix in the shared GL layer is your call.
- **Setup:** I worked on a plain branch in the main checkout rather than a worktree, as nothing else was using it.

Want me to push and open a draft PR?

File a ticket for a proper GL_POLYGON fix.  Most of these look good, but DeepStars barely shows anything. Like, maybe 3 stars are on screen at a time, and they never smear.  Probably should take it out of the rotation if we can't get the desired effect.

TinyGL here is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), so a hack that calls `glBegin(GL_POLYGON)` draws nothing. Issue #80 fixed `GL_LINE_LOOP` (which the same switch compiled out) and left polygons as "each hack works round it".

## Current state

Three wrappers map it to a triangle fan locally:

- `hacks/rubik_gl.c` (with a polygon offset for its decals)
- `hacks/menger_gl.c`
- `hacks/superquadrics_single_gl.c`

`buildlwo.c` (Pipes) does the same in its own wrapper. Without the mapping Menger and Superquadrics render black (found in the 2026-10-18 GL batch).

## Why a proper fix

The same `glBegin` macro is copied into every wrapper, and every unported GL hack that uses `GL_POLYGON` will hit it: circuit, dolphin, maze3d, polytopes, polyhedra-gl, shark, sonar, sproingies, topblock, whale. A hack that nobody wraps just draws black, and the host tests only notice if the hack has a "draws something" check.

## Options

1. Patch TinyGL (`tools/tinygl_patch.py`) to handle `GL_POLYGON` itself, as a fan from the first vertex. Exact for convex polygons, which is every use I have seen in the vendored hacks. Needs the same guard as the line loop patch, so an unhandled primitive cannot overrun the vertex slots.

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `entire trail merge <trail>` (the trail
  number, not the PR number; omit it on the trail's branch) once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). `entire trail merge` checks the gates first and
  merges nothing while one fails or is pending; `--dry-run` reports which.
  Rod's approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire Gates check to finish.
  If the only failing gates are Approvals (he approved in chat) or a stacked
  PR's "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges, and the PR is
  mergeable, try `entire trail merge <trail> --force --yes` with no rebase;
  the bypass is recorded on the trail. The repo's bypass policy is now
  "nobody", so it is refused ("does not allow bypassing gates", PR #132):
  do not merge round it with `gh pr merge`. Ask Rod to approve the trail in
  the Entire UI, then run a plain `entire trail merge`. For any other failing
  gate, stop and tell Rod.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A trail's "N commits behind" can understate: trail 66 said 1 and its branch
  was 17 behind. Count with `git rev-list --count <branch>..origin/main`
  before a cherry-pick, and re-apply by hand if the files conflict.
- To read another agent's session, run `entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint>
  --full` (or `--transcript` for the JSONL) from the repo root: elsewhere it
  says "not a git repository". `entire session info <id>` knows only local
  sessions, so find the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain <sha>` on
  one of the agent's commits.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,

  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase

  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers

- `entire trail finding list` can show one open "Review verdict ... approve"

  repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/commits/<branch>/check-runs

- If `entire trail create` reports "failed to push branch", run
  `git push -u origin <branch>` and rerun it: the trail is then created.
- Run `gh pr ready N` and `entire trail merge <trail>` as separate commands:
  on a PR that is already ready, `ready` exits non-zero and skips a chained
  merge.
  Confirm with `gh pr view N --json state`.
- `entire trail merge <trail> --dry-run` can say "findings pending: Waiting

Written by an agent (Claude) running under Rod's direction.

## What this adds

Seven GL hacks on the TinyGL layer, each the unmodified xscreensaver source
built through a `USE_GL` wrapper: GLMatrix, CubeStack, Kaleidocycle,
DangerBall, Cubenetic, Superquadrics and Menger. DeepStars was ported too, and
Rod dropped it after seeing it on the panel (about three dim stars, no smear);
its source, wrapper and notices row stay, and it is in `failed_ports.txt`.

| Hack | On the board (45 s windows) | Wrapper work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GLMatrix | 13-44 fps, about 17 once full (6 as copied) | alpha folded into colour, half size, density 12, 10 ms delay, single precision |
| CubeStack | 17-38 fps | 10 ms delay |
| Kaleidocycle | 30-35 fps | 10 ms delay |
| DangerBall | 24-26 fps | 10 ms delay |
| Cubenetic | 12-18 fps (1.2 as copied) | 64 by 64 texture, single precision, frees its cube array |
| Superquadrics | 14-27 fps (8-11 as copied) | triangle fans for `GL_POLYGON`, half size, single precision |
| Menger | 13-44 fps | triangle fans for `GL_POLYGON`, half size, `*maxDepth: 2` |

## Notes for review

- GLMatrix keeps its look in alpha, which TinyGL lacks. The wrapper
  premultiplies the glyph texture as it uploads and scales `glColor4f`; an
  additive blend cannot tell the difference. `matrix3.png` is deflated at build
  time by `gl_textures.py`, never committed.
- Cubenetic's plasma texture was 847 ms a frame at 256 by 256.
  `tools/cubenetic_patch.py` makes the size a build setting (64 by 64).
- The restart leak test found a real upstream leak in Cubenetic (320 bytes a
  start); the wrapper frees it.
- Superquadrics and Menger drew nothing because TinyGL has no `GL_POLYGON`
  (issue #80). Each wrapper draws a fan, as Rubik does. A shared fix is filed
  as #138; I did not touch the shared GL layer.
- Registry overrides: `*delay: 10000` for the six that were paced by their own
  delay (the loop credits only the push against it), `*density: 12` for
  GLMatrix, `*maxDepth: 2` for Menger.
- Menger's frame rate swings 13-44 fps: the low end is while a depth level's
  display list is built.

## Verified

- Host: `pio test -e native` passes, 860 of 860, before DeepStars was dropped;
  after it, `test_hacks` passes, 138 of 138. `uv run pytest tools/tests` and
  `check_notices.py` pass.
- Pinned frame hashes were taken after looking at the frames. Mutation checks
  were caught: GLMatrix's alpha and colour folds, both polygon-fan mappings,
  and Cubenetic's free.
- Device: flashed and measured with `flash_and_capture.sh`, one 45 s lap for

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

cat > tools/superquadrics_patch.py <<'EOF'
"""Keeps Superquadrics's random index below its range.

Upstream's `myrand` multiplies in `float`, so the largest value `LRAND()` can
return (2147483647) rounds up to 2^31 and `myrand(4)` is 4, which then indexes
`pats[4][t]` in a 4 by 4 array. The build (firmware/patch_float_literals.py)
runs this on the hack's text; the copied superquadrics.c stays byte-identical.
The replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build.
"""

OLD = "\treturn ((int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND)));\n"
NEW = (
    "\tint r = (int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND));\n"
    "\treturn r < range ? r : range - 1;\n"
)


def keep_myrand_in_range(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD.strip()}` in superquadrics.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)
EOF
cat > tools/tests/test_superquadrics_patch.py <<'EOF'
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import superquadrics_patch as sp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "glx" / "superquadrics.c"

SAMPLE = """\
static int
myrand(int range)
{
\treturn ((int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND)));
}
"""


def test_the_random_index_is_clamped():
    out = sp.keep_myrand_in_range(SAMPLE)
    assert "return r < range ? r : range - 1;" in out
    assert "((float) range) * LRAND()" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_that_has_changed():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        sp.keep_myrand_in_range(SAMPLE.replace("(float) range", "(double) range"))


def _myrand_at_the_top_of_the_range(tmp_path: Path, source: str, range_: int) -> int:
    body = re.search(r"static int\nmyrand\(int range\)\n\{.*?\n\}\n", source, re.S)
    assert body
    program = (
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        "#define LRAND() 2147483647L\n"
        "#define MAXRAND (2147483648.0)\n"
        f"{body.group(0)}"
        f'int main(void) {{ printf("%d", myrand({range_})); return 0; }}\n'
    )
    c = tmp_path / "myrand.c"
    c.write_text(program)
    exe = tmp_path / "myrand"
    subprocess.run(["cc", "-o", str(exe), str(c)], check=True)
    return int(subprocess.run([str(exe)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
@pytest.mark.parametrize("range_", [2, 3, 4, 100, 200])
def test_the_largest_random_value_stays_below_the_range(tmp_path, range_):
    patched = sp.keep_myrand_in_range(UPSTREAM.read_text())
    assert _myrand_at_the_top_of_the_range(tmp_path, patched, range_) == range_ - 1


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_upstream_returns_the_range_itself_there(tmp_path):
    assert _myrand_at_the_top_of_the_range(tmp_path, UPSTREAM.read_text(), 4) == 4
EOF

The Superquadrics finding is fixed and marked resolved on trail 83. Nothing is committed yet.

- **Cause:** the reviewer was right, and upstream has it too. `myrand` multiplies in `float`, so when `LRAND()` returns 2147483647 it rounds up to 2147483648 and `myrand(4)` returns 4. `MakeUpStuff` then reads one row past the end of `pats[4][4]`.
- **Fix:** `tools/superquadrics_patch.py` clamps the result below `range` at build time. The build runs it through `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, so the copied hack stays byte-identical. The generated source has the clamp. I checked that by reading the generated file, not by running a frame.
- **Test:** `tools/tests/test_superquadrics_patch.py` compiles the real `myrand` with `LRAND()` fixed at 2147483647. Upstream's version returns 4 there, which reproduces the bug, and the patched version returns `range - 1` for ranges 2, 3, 4, 100 and 200. Reverting the clamp makes the test fail. I wrote the patch and the test together, so I didn't watch the test fail before the fix, but the upstream check shows the bug.
- **Checks:** `test_hacks` passes (140 of 140) and the tools tests pass (612). The frame pins didn't move.
- **Docs:** I added a line to `.claude/rules/hacks.md`.

I didn't flash the board, since only the build path changed and the clamp can't alter a frame unless the random value is the one-in-two-billion case.
